extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of art history, censorship, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarizing the creation, reception, controversies, reproduction, and later provenance of a single painting (Paul Émile Chabas's September Morn). Covers artistic style, Salon reception, censorship episodes, and popular culture effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity definition for visual works
rubrics_metrics.description: Images of adults and children meant to 'provoke, incite, or stimulate debauchery' were targeted by laws against pornography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites late-19th/early-20th-century legal standards that judged images obscene if intended to arouse sexual behavior or lust; this standard was used to decide what printed or imported images could be suppressed. (Original phrasing: 'images of adults and children meant to "provoke, incite, or stimulate debauchery".')

rubrics_metrics.name: Tariff/import restriction on obscene art
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tariff of 1842 banned the importing of foreign works of art deemed obscene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, U.S. customs policy could be used to prevent entry of works considered obscene; commercial importation was a regulatory vector for censoring visual art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum versus commercial reproduction distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Museums could hold works depicting nudity, but commercial works (including photographs of artwork) could be—and were—confiscated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that institutions displaying art were sometimes treated differently from commercial sellers; location and mode of distribution (museum exhibition vs. commercial sale/print) influenced enforcement decisions and public acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display-location and audience-sensitivity standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities objected to public display of nude images where children could see them; Chicago's mayor proposed and city council imposed fines for displaying nude art along public roads and in places frequented by children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical enforcement often turned on whether an image was publicly visible to minors; local ordinances (example: $25–100 fine in Chicago) and prosecutions targeted storefront displays and other public venues accessible to children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal and distribution restrictions on reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Postcards bearing the painting were banned from the postal system; possession or display of reproductions risked confiscation and fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators used postal rules and local police action to restrict circulation of popular reproductions, not only original paintings. The article gives multiple examples of arrests, confiscations, and bans tied to reproductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship mitigation by artistic status
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's status as 'a work of art' and the artist's reputation could protect it from prosecution or harsher enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes disagreement among historians about why legal action was sometimes not pursued (e.g., Comstock not prosecuting); one explanation is that established artistic status and being shown as 'art' reduced the likelihood of legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic nude conventions as artistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In academic art the models were idealized: body hair of women would not be shown, and the pubic area was rendered smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes stylistic and normative standards for producing 'acceptable' academic nudes in late-19th/early-20th-century French Salon practice; such conventions could influence critics' and censors' readings of a work's intent and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salon/critical evaluation criteria (technique and composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary Salon reviewers praised qualities such as 'purity' of drawing, 'remarkable delicacy' of modeling, tonal dominance (grays evoking morning), and 'delicately composed' imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical reception at the Paris Salon centered on technical execution, tonality, composition and the evocation of mood; reviewers' language (e.g., 'rare purity', 'indisputable charm') indicates the aesthetic dimensions used to judge the painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive/prudential criteria for acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether a subject's pose represents protecting modesty, being cold, sponge bathing, or a fetishisation of innocence affected judgments of propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of the depicted gesture and posture informed arguments for or against the painting's decency: readings that emphasized innocence or bath-preparation tended to defend it, while readings that sexualized the pose supported censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical censorship techniques applied to reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper or shop reproductions were sometimes censored by painting in clothing or otherwise altering prints to make them less explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and exhibitors used ad-hoc visual modifications (e.g., 'the Star artist has painted in a short petticoat') to avoid violating community standards while still reproducing an image, showing an applied, pragmatic rubric for acceptable depiction in mass media.
